questions.topic: Analytical writing — TEAL paragraphs and line of argument
questions.prompt: ANALYTICAL PRACTICE — Write one developed paragraph responding to: How might a playwright make a manipulative antagonist appear trustworthy to other characters but threatening to the audience? Use an imagined example rather than a quotation from Othello.

markPoints: close explanation of how the method creates two different impressions
connection to audience knowledge or dramatic irony
link back to the line of argument
answer.modelAnswer: A playwright can make a manipulative antagonist dangerous by giving him a credible public persona while privately revealing his strategy to the audience. If other characters repeatedly praise his honesty, that reputation becomes a form of dramatic irony: the audience recognises that trust is precisely what allows him to control them. A private aside exposing his plan would widen the gap between public appearance and private intention, making apparently ordinary advice feel threatening.

feedback.short: Suggested answer: A playwright can make a manipulative antagonist dangerous by giving him a credible public persona while privately revealing his strategy to the audience. If other characters repeatedly praise his honesty, that reputation becomes a form of dramatic irony: the audience recognises that trust is precisely what allows him to control them. A private aside exposing his plan would widen the gap between public appearance and private intention, making apparently ordinary advice feel threatening.
steps: Use the task requirements as a checklist before writing.
Criterion 1: clear analytical claim.
Criterion 2: specific method or imagined evidence.
Criterion 3: close explanation of how the method creates two different impressions.
Criterion 4: connection to audience knowledge or dramatic irony.
Criterion 5: link back to the line of argument.
feedback.commonError: Writing fluently but missing one or more explicit task requirements.
feedback.remember: Success checklist: clear analytical claim; specific method or imagined evidence; close explanation of how the method creates two different impressions; connection to audience knowledge or dramatic irony; link back to the line of argument.

note.title: Analytical writing — TEAL paragraphs and line of argument
note.overview: Build concise analytical paragraphs that sustain an interpretation instead of listing quotations and techniques.
learningGoals: Form a debatable line of argument.
Select evidence that supports a precise claim.
Link paragraph reasoning back to the argument.
mustMemoriseRules: Claim first: know what you are trying to prove.
Evidence is a starting point for analysis, not the end.
Name a method only when the label helps explain meaning.
Context must illuminate the textual argument.
workedExamples: Claim → focused evidence/reference → analysis of specific choice → significance → return to argument.
A method label earns little by itself; the explanation of how and why it works matters.
commonMistakes: Using long quotation as a substitute for analysis.
Changing interpretation from paragraph to paragraph without a coherent argument.
detailedExplanation: The curriculum scope and assessed skills are verified against the official Tiffin Girls’ School Year 9 English Curriculum Outline 2026-27.
Plot and method questions support the school focus on Othello and Iago; longer paragraph tasks are app practice, not the teacher’s live timed assessment.
Long open responses do not by themselves create formal Mastery evidence.
examTips: Use plot knowledge only when it supports an interpretation.
Distinguish what characters believe from what the audience knows.
Analyse Shakespeare’s method rather than attaching labels.
Keep a coherent line of argument.
quickCheck: Form a debatable line of argument.
Select evidence that supports a precise claim.
Link paragraph reasoning back to the argument.
beforeStartingPractice: Recall the character relationships and central deception before practice.
